newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian minister calls for stable world tea prices.
newsitem.headline: Indian minister calls for stable world tea prices.

text.p: India's commerce minister B.B. Ramaiah on Monday urged tea producers to come together and formulate a common strategy to bring stability to world tea prices.
"I have held a dialogue with Kenya in this regard," Ramaiah told a planters' conference in the southern Indian town of Coonoor.
"If we can succeed in our efforts, tea prices in world markets can stabilise." He did not elaborate.
Ramaiah said the Indian tea industry should look at the possibility of exporting more value-added products.
"Brand names and brand equity are very important to boost exports. We can gain substantially," he said speaking at the two-day conference, which opened on Sunday.
The conference is sponsored by the United Planters' Association of Southern India (UPASI).
The minister said his ministry would take up with the Reserve Bank of India and the finance ministry the issue of extending to Indian exporters credit facilities which would help Russian buyers.

Conference delegates said Sri Lanka, another major producer and the world's biggest tea exporter, had entrenched itself in export markets in Russia and the CIS (Commonwealth of Independent States) by offering easy credit terms to buyers there.
"The tea industry needs proper support," Ramaiah said.
India's tea exports have fallen sharply since 1991 following the collapse of the Soviet Union which accounted for nearly 50 percent of its export.
Tea exports last year totalled 163.7 million kgs, slightly up from 150.7 million kgs in the previous year and compared to 215 million in 1991.
Earlier, UPASI President S. Samuel said that India's plantation crops - tea, coffee, cardamom and pepper - accounted for annual export earnings of 28 billion rupees.

The government had set up production targets for tea and coffee of one billion kgs and 300,000 tonnes respectively by the year 2000, against the current output level of 750 million and 200,000 respectively which were too ambitious, he said.
While increasing production was most desirable, investments were needed to raise quality to maintain international competitiveness through research, Samuel said.
"Very little is being done in generic promotion of tea as a health drink," he said.
